# Ego Dissolution as Consciousness-Widening, Not Moralism

## The Room That Got Too Big for the Furniture

Picture a single chair in the middle of a vast empty hall. It's a perfectly good chair. But the hall is so large that the chair barely registers — it doesn't fill the room, doesn't dominate it, doesn't even draw the eye. Nobody had to take the chair away. The room simply grew until the chair stopped mattering.

That's how the ego actually thins in Aurobindo's account of the siddhis. You don't fight the chair. You don't scrub it, shame it, or saw off its legs. You let the room expand until the narrow "me" no longer fits the space and stops running the show on its own.[^1] Sraddhalu is blunt about it: the usual spiritual instruction — *first purify yourself, remove your desire, then you may use the power* — is a way of looking at the thing, but only "indirectly and by secondary symptoms." Look at the underlying principle, he says, and it has nothing to do with morality. "It's not about petty egoism getting inflated from a moral point of view."[^2] The ego doesn't dissolve because you got good. It dissolves because you got *wide*.

## What This Actually Is

This is the load-bearing mechanism under the entire safe-use teaching. Aurobindo's second fixed principle for the siddhis reads: the powers "can manifest fully only when we leave ego and offer up our petty separate being in the vastness of God's being."[^3] Everyone hears that and assumes it's a moral demand — be humble, be selfless, earn it. It isn't. The reason your narrow self blocks the power is *geometric*, not ethical. A small consciousness is finite. The full operation of a knowledge-power or a will-power is, in its true form, infinite — it reaches as far as God's being reaches. Run an infinite operation through a narrow pipe and you get exactly what Aurobindo describes: partial, defective, even deceptive output, "because it's mixed."[^4]

Sraddhalu stops mid-talk to nail down what Aurobindo is *not* saying. "He's not saying anything about you must grow in consciousness. He's only saying you must become vast in God's being."[^5] And the misuse worry — "Oh, I will misuse it" — gets explicitly set aside: "Yes, that also is there. But the full operation is not there because oh I will misuse or not. It has nothing to do with that. It's not a moral or ethical thing... It's about your narrow consciousness limiting its full operation."[^6] The block is the narrowness itself. Widen, and the full operation becomes possible — "and it's still nature's operation," not a reward dispensed for good behavior.

So the page names a pattern that runs against the grain of most ego-work: **dissolution by expansion, not by subtraction.** You don't remove the self. You out-scale it.

## The Mechanism: Thinning by Widening

Here's the move, deconstructed. A narrow ego isn't a quantity of badness to be reduced toward zero. It's a *boundary* — a small circle drawn around "what is me." Everything inside the circle feels personal and urgent; everything outside feels foreign. Moralistic ego-work attacks the contents of the circle: less vanity, less desire, less grasping. It leaves the circle's *size* untouched. You can spend a lifetime polishing a small circle and still be small.

The widening move ignores the contents entirely and works on the radius. When the circle grows — and grows until it opens onto "an infinite wideness which is the vastness of God's being," because Aurobindo insists any lesser wideness is just "big finite," still bounded[^7] — the ratio of "me" to "everything" collapses toward nothing. The chair in the hall. You haven't suppressed a single desire. You've simply made the desire small relative to the room, so it stops steering. Sraddhalu's phrase: "your narrow person automatically thins because now you feel everybody's thing as yours."[^8] *Automatically* is the operative word. The thinning is a side effect of scale, not a result of effort against the self.

And the direction of travel matters enormously. There are two ways to "get bigger," and only one of them works. The asura's way: "I make myself larger and larger and dominate more and wider and impose more and more."[^9] That's the ego inflating — annexing more territory while keeping itself at the center. It fails by construction, because the center never moves; you've just built a bigger empire around the same small king. The real way runs the opposite direction: the vastness already exists "within you, above you, in the divine consciousness," and you don't seize it — "you relax and open to it, invite it, let it fill you and give yourself to it. It draws you into itself, into its vastness, and you merge with it."[^10] Note the verbs. Relax. Open. Invite. Give. Merge. Every one is a *release* of effort, not an application of it. Aurobindo calls this "the fastest, most rapid way" — and the petty separate being thins out because it's been drawn into something larger than it, not crushed by something stronger than it.[^11]

One more piece, because it's a real hazard: even a thinned ego can pop back up. The narrow self isn't deleted; it's de-centered, and a de-centered thing can re-center the instant attention slips. A power flowers, something extraordinary happens, and the "me" lunges back in to claim it — *I did that.* This is precisely why the widening can never be a one-time graduation. It has to be ongoing, because the chair is still in the room; it only stops mattering as long as the room stays big.

## What This Gives the Rest of the Vault

This page supplies the *engine* that the safe-use framework keeps referring to. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/four-principles-of-safe-siddhi-use|The four principles of safe siddhi use]] state the second principle — leave ego, offer the petty being into vastness — but state it as a rule. This page explains *why the rule is structural rather than moral*, which is the difference between a commandment you obey and a mechanism you operate.

It also disarms a specific danger documented elsewhere. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/siddhi-danger-triangle-fragmentation-weak-adhara-egoism|The siddhi danger triangle]] shows that powers become destructive when they run fragmentarily through a weak, ego-dominated vehicle. The triangle names the disease; this page names the cure — and crucially, the cure is *not* "have less ego" (which is just willpower against a circle) but "be wider," which dissolves the ego-domination as a byproduct. And it gives a positive diagnostic to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/signs-the-siddhis-are-unfolding|the signs the siddhis are unfolding]]: if your powers are getting smoother, more complete, less distorted, the real reason is that your consciousness has been quietly widening — "the functioning of these powers is smooth, natural and more and more complete in proportion as you are more and more in this consciousness."[^12] Smoothness is a readout of width.

Finally it grounds the whole batch's relationship to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/vyapti-receptive-and-communicative|vyapti]], because Aurobindo's own illustration of widening is a vyapti gradient — which the case study walks through next.

## Case Study: The Small, the Large, and the Vast on a Crowded Bus

Aurobindo and Sraddhalu don't argue the widening abstractly. They walk it up through four stages of one specific power — vyapti, the reception of others' inner states — and you can feel the ego thin at each rung.[^13]

**Small.** You're a small consciousness and you meet someone with a strong vital. You feel the pressure of their force on you. If they're strong enough, they get you to say yes when you came to say no — and here's the cruelty of it, "you will like it. You will want it." You walk away grateful: "Oh, thank God I said yes, I had thought to come and say no." That's how you know it worked — they changed your state and overcame your own resistance, and you never noticed.[^14] At this level you're a puppet who doesn't even know you're on strings. The ego is total here precisely because it's so small: it has no room to see anything outside itself, so it experiences a hijack as a free choice.

**Partially widened.** Now you've grown a little. The same pressure hits, but this time something registers: "Hey, how did that happen? I still want to say no but I can't. What is this magic of influence?"[^15] You can't stop it yet, but you can *see* it. The circle has grown just enough to include the edge of the manipulation in its field of view. This is the dangerous middle — aware enough to feel violated, not wide enough to be free.

**Large.** Widen further and the perception generalizes. It's no longer just the overwhelming person — you start feeling the daydreamer beside you, the stranger's quiet distress, "because your consciousness is larger and you experience them as if inside you." You sit in a library or a bus next to someone in severe depression, ride for half an hour, and arrive at the office inexplicably depressed: "I don't know what happened this morning, I was so bright. By the time I've reached the office I'm severely depressed."[^16] You caught the infection without consent. Still overwhelmed — but now, when you're conscious, you can at least name the source: "Oh, it is this person, and I'm feeling the influence entering me."[^17] Empathy has arrived, and with it the new problem of porous boundaries.

**Vast.** Now the room opens all the way. A "distant influence of the self" is felt — "a great vast peace... a solidity of freedom" — and inside that peace all the same states are still perceived, but you have "the freedom with the sensitivity, the ability to be unoverwhelmed without losing the perception itself."[^18] You feel the stranger's grief, but it doesn't capsize you, because it's small relative to the vastness you're seated in. And then the power inverts: feeling someone's state from *inside* that width, "the intention and the shift in your consciousness is enough to actually lift them from that state."[^19] Not a technique, not a strain — "as if in a physical hand you would reach out to a child who's weeping... except you don't need a physical hand for that."[^20] At this rung the ego thins on its own, because "now you feel everybody's thing as yours" and "your own suffering you realize is just part of a larger universal working" — so you stop giving it disproportionate weight.[^21]

The point of the worked example: nobody at the vast rung *tried* to be less egotistical than the puppet at the small rung. The vast person's ego thinned as a free consequence of the room growing. Same power, four sizes of self, and the moral quality tracked the width the whole way down.

## Implementation — The Moment of Letting Yourself Be Drawn In

You notice the reflex first. Something good is starting to move through you — a clear intuition, a sense that you could shift the mood of this room, a power flowering at the edge of you — and immediately the old engine fires: *grab it, run it harder, make it bigger, make it yours.* You can feel the muscle tense. That's the asura's move, the inflation: I'll become larger and larger and dominate more. Your jaw sets. Your attention narrows to a point on the prize. And right there, watch what happens — the operation gets choppy, partial, mixed. The harder you push, the more it deceives you.

So you stop pushing. Literally let the effort fall. There's a vastness already above you and within you — you don't manufacture it, you don't earn it, it's simply there, larger than the small thing trying to seize the prize. You turn toward it the way you'd lean back into water you trust to hold you. You don't grab the vastness either — you can't; the small can't seize the large. You open. You invite. *Come in. Fill this.* And then the quiet, slightly vertiginous part: you give yourself to it. You let it draw you. Not you climbing up into it — it pulling you in, the way a current takes you when you stop swimming against it.

For a second the narrow you protests — *but then who's in charge?* — and you feel the chair in the empty hall, still there, just no longer the size of the room. The grief of the stranger across the bus is in your field now, and so is half the city's mood, and none of it tips you, because you're seated in something too wide to tip. The intuition completes itself clean. You turn toward the person you wanted to help and the wish to lift them *is* the lifting — no hand, no strain, just the shift. And you notice, almost in passing, that the "me" that was so desperate to own this a minute ago has gone quiet. You didn't silence it. You just got bigger than it. The whole move took less effort than the grab would have. That's the tell that you did it right: it felt like release, not conquest.

## When the Widening Fails: The Inflation That Looks Like Growth

The signature failure has a specific flavor, and it's seductive because it *feels* like progress. You're getting bigger — but you're getting bigger the asura's way. More reach, more influence, more domination, a wider empire — with the same small king dead-center, narrating the whole thing as *mine*. The diagnostic: ask whether the center moved. Real widening de-centers the self; inflation expands the territory while leaving the self firmly at the middle. If you can still locate a sharp "I" at the hub of the expansion, claiming the gains, you've inflated, not widened. Aurobindo flags exactly this — you can become "quite wide, even vitally wide, mentally wide," and it's still finite, "big finite," not the real wideness at all.[^22] A big finite ego is more dangerous than a small one, because it has more power and the same possessiveness.

The second failure is the pop-back. You did widen, the room grew, the chair stopped mattering — and then a siddhi flowered, something undeniable happened, and the narrow self lunged back in to seize the experience and stamp its name on it. The signs: a sudden sense of "I am a very great man indeed," a hunger to repeat the feat, a possessiveness about the power. The thinned ego didn't die; it re-centered the instant your attention drifted. This is why "leave ego" can never be a finished task. The room only stays big while you keep it open, and the moment you coast, the walls come back in.

The third, quietest failure is mistaking moral effort for the actual work — grinding away at desire and vanity, scrubbing the chair, and wondering why the power stays partial. You're working on the contents of the circle and leaving its radius untouched. You can become a genuinely better person this way and still have a narrow consciousness throttling every power that tries to run through it. The fix isn't more scrubbing. It's the radius.

## Evidence, Tensions, and Open Questions

The whole teaching rests on a transcript of Sraddhalu reading and unpacking Aurobindo's *Record of Yoga* notes, so every claim here is `[PARAPHRASED]`, with the principle-statements marked closer to Aurobindo's own words where read aloud.[^23] That's a real evidentiary limit: we have a practitioner-teacher's gloss on a private spiritual diary, not a controlled account.

The sharpest internal tension is one Sraddhalu raises himself and does not fully resolve. He concedes that "purify yourself first, then use the power" is a valid way of looking at it — "but indirectly and by secondary symptoms."[^24] So is the moral model *wrong*, or is it a low-resolution description of the same event? If widening automatically thins the ego, and a thinned ego *looks* purified, then the moralist and Aurobindo might be pointing at one phenomenon from two angles — the moralist watching the symptom (less vanity), Aurobindo describing the cause (more width). The page takes the position that width is causal and morality is downstream, but it should be flagged that this is an interpretive commitment, not a settled fact.

A second open question: the "automatic" claim. Aurobindo says the ego thins *automatically* as consciousness widens. But the pop-back hazard implies the automaticity isn't permanent — the ego can re-seize. So is the thinning automatic-but-reversible, requiring constant maintenance, or is there a threshold of width past which the seizure can no longer happen? The transcript suggests the former and gestures at the latter without committing.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Follow the moralist's path — the tapas-and-purification road the vault knows well from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/heat-generation-tapas-state|tapas]] and the renunciate ascetic ideal — and your days fill with a particular kind of labor. You watch desire arise and you deny it. You catch vanity and you shame it. You burn the impurity off through heat and discipline, and the self gets smaller, cleaner, harder, year by year. The felt texture is *friction*: you are always working against something in yourself, and the progress is measured in what you've subtracted. It's real, and it can take you a long way. But notice — you could do all of it and still be operating a small circle. You'd be a purer narrow self.

Walk Aurobindo's path instead and the daily texture is almost the opposite — *release* rather than friction. You're not subtracting anything. You're leaning back into a vastness that's already there and letting it draw you in. The desire and the vanity haven't been hunted down; they've simply gone quiet because they shrank relative to the room. What you'd experience is not the satisfaction of a hard-won purity but the strange lightness of a self that stopped mattering without ever being attacked. The two paths can even produce the same downstream look — a person less driven by ego — but one got there by grinding the chair down and the other by enlarging the hall, and the second one is, Aurobindo insists, the faster road.

Now stand both of those next to the Buddhist anattā route — the no-self teaching — and a third texture appears. The anattā path investigates the chair until you see there was never a solid chair there at all; the self is examined into transparency, recognized as a process with no owner at the center. Sit with that and the relief is *insight*: the burden of self-ownership drops because you see through the one who was carrying it. Aurobindo's path doesn't deny the self this way — the petty separate being is real enough; it just gets out-scaled and drawn up into something larger rather than seen through. Experientially the difference is sharp. The anattā practitioner ends with *no one home and that's the freedom.* The Aurobindonian ends with *someone vast at home, and the small one folded into it.* One dissolves the self by analysis into emptiness; the other dissolves it by merger into fullness. The vault's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/siddhis-and-the-attainment-trap|attainment-trap]] material warns that chasing the power inflates the very ego you meant to lose — and both the emptiness route and the fullness route answer that warning, but they hand you opposite-feeling medicines for the same wound: one empties the cup, the other overflows it.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Psychology — the self-boundary and its dissolution.** The vault's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/flow-state-intensity|Flow State Intensity]] page describes the moment the self disappears into a task — action and awareness merge, self-consciousness drops, the doer stops being separate from the doing. Neuroscience locates a correlate of this in attenuation of the default-mode network, the brain's self-referential idling circuit; quiet the DMN and the felt boundary of "me" loosens, in flow and in the deeper ego-dissolution states. Lay Aurobindo's mechanism alongside it and something clicks that neither account states alone. The flow page insists, against pop psychology, that the *valuable* self-loss is the kind *earned through prior ordeal* — tapas first, then the boundary drops. That's the moralist's sequencing exactly: purify, then permit. Aurobindo's claim cuts the other way — the self-loss isn't earned by prior work on the self, it's a *byproduct of widening the field of consciousness*, and it can precede the purification rather than follow it. The insight the pairing produces: these may be two thresholds on the same dial. Flow attenuates the boundary *within a task* (the room grows only as wide as the activity); Aurobindo's widening attenuates it *without an object*, opening to vastness with no task at all. Flow is ego-dissolution rented by absorption and repossessed the moment the task ends — which is exactly Sraddhalu's pop-back, the ego re-seizing when attention drifts. The unsolved question both share: is the DMN-quiet a *result* of effortful skill (the earned-flow thesis) or a *result of releasing effort entirely* (Aurobindo's relax-open-invite)? The vault's own flow page bets on earned; Aurobindo bets on released. Same neural floor, opposite ladders.

This handshake also clarifies the vault's own internal disagreement. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/surrender-and-ego-death|Surrender and Ego-Death]] frames the drop of the ego as a surrender — a giving-up. Aurobindo agrees on the verb (offer up, give yourself, let it draw you) but disagrees on the *target*: you don't surrender *to nothing*, you surrender *into a vastness*. The death is a merger, not an annihilation. That distinction — dissolution-as-emptying versus dissolution-as-being-drawn-into-fullness — is precisely the seam the psychology pages can't resolve from inside psychology, because it's a claim about *what's on the other side of the boundary*, which the DMN data is silent on. The eastern-spirituality frame supplies the missing half: it specifies the destination of the dissolution.

**Behavioral-mechanics — why a wide consciousness can't be played.** Read the small-rung of Aurobindo's vyapti gradient — the puppet who says yes and is grateful for it — next to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/resistance-frame-defense|Resistance and Frame Defense]] and the convergence is almost eerie. The influence operator works by getting their frame to land before you've registered the probe: the manipulation succeeds precisely *to the degree the target's consciousness is too small to see the wave arriving.* Frame defense, in the behavioral literature, is a set of *techniques* — response moves you deploy to hold your frame under challenge. Aurobindo describes the same protection arriving by a completely different route: not technique, but *width*. At the small rung you're hijacked and grateful. At the partially-widened rung you feel the manipulation but can't stop it — "what is this magic of influence?" — which maps exactly onto the half-trained operator who can name the frame attack but still loses ground. At the large and vast rungs the influence wave is perceived *impersonally*, as just one more state crossing a field too wide to be captured by it, and the manipulation simply fails to find a small enough "me" to grab. The insight neither domain reaches alone: frame defense and consciousness-widening are the *same capacity at two altitudes.* The behavioral version is a learned skill you run against a specific opponent in a specific encounter; the contemplative version is a standing width that defends every frame against every probe at once, without a technique, because there's no narrow target left to push on. And it runs the other way too — the manipulation literature accidentally proves Aurobindo's mechanism. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/frame-control-and-archetypes|Frame control]] works by shrinking the target's effective field to the operator's chosen frame; the entire craft of influence is *induced narrowness*. So the strongest empirical evidence that width is protective is the documented fact that the influence operator's first job is always to make you small. Widen, and the whole apparatus of persuasion loses its purchase — not because you got morally stronger, but because, as on the bus, you became too vast to puppet.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication:** The single most important move in safe siddhi development is not a moral one. Every effort spent suppressing desire and scrubbing vanity is working on the *contents* of the self while leaving its *radius* untouched — and the radius is what throttles the power. The leverage is entirely in the widening; the purity is a side effect that shows up downstream on its own.

**Generative questions:**
- If the moral model is a "secondary symptom" reading of the widening, is there *any* case where moral purification is genuinely causal and not just downstream — or is virtue always an effect of width and never a cause?
- The ego can pop back up and re-seize an experience. Is there a threshold of width past which re-seizure becomes structurally impossible, or is the vastness always a tenancy that must be continually renewed?
- Flow rents self-loss through absorption in a task; Aurobindo's widening opens it without an object. Can the objectless widening be *trained*, the way flow can be engineered through challenge-skill matching — or does training it reintroduce the asura's grab?

# Nyāsa: Installing the Mantra in the Body

## Touch, Sound, Place: Loading a God Into Your Own Hands

Watch the hands first. The practitioner touches thumb to each fingertip in turn, then presses palm to forehead, to mouth, to heart, to shoulders, to the eyes, to the crown — each touch landing with a syllable. *Na* — the thumb. *Ma* — the index. *Śi* — the middle. It looks like a private sign language, or, as Selvalingam puts it, like a dancer locking a move, "rap and lock."[^1] What's actually happening is stranger and simpler than it looks: the practitioner is taking a mantra apart syllable by syllable and *placing* each piece into a specific part of the body.

That's nyāsa. The word means "placing" or "depositing." You take *na-ma-śi-vā-ya*, the five syllables of Śiva, and you install them — into fingers, into limbs, into the centers of the body — until the body itself is the mantra. Selvalingam calls it the heart of the whole Tantric tradition, and his one-line reason cuts to it: nyāsa is "about feeling divinity in your own body."[^2] Not picturing a god across the room. Feeling the god land in your own hand.

## What This Actually Is

Nyāsa is the ritual act of installing mantra-syllables into the body by touch and intention.[^3] You assign each syllable of the mantra to a location, touch that location while sounding (or silently intoning) the syllable, and in doing so you "deposit" the divine power of that syllable there.

Selvalingam walks two specific forms with the five-syllable Śiva mantra.[^4]

**Kara-nyāsa** — hand-installation. The five bīja syllables *na-ma-śi-vā-ya* are placed onto the fingers. You touch each syllable into a finger in sequence, charging the hand. The hand becomes the field where the mantra first lives — which is why the gestures look like a tight, deliberate hand-dance.

**Ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa** — six-limb installation. The mantra is then placed onto six "limbs" of the body — heart, head, crown-tuft, armor (shoulders/torso), the three eyes, and the weapon (a clap or snap that seals the field). Six placements, six touches, the same syllables now distributed across the whole frame so the entire body is mapped to the mantra.[^5]

The key move in both: you are not *thinking about* Śiva. You are *touching* Śiva into yourself. The mantra stops being a sound in the air or an image in the mind and becomes a felt charge in the tissue — a god you can locate by pressing on your own chest.

## The Logic of Placing: Why Touch Closes the Loop

Why touch? Why not just chant, or visualize? The internal logic is about closing a loop that sound and image leave open.

A chanted mantra lives in the air and the ear — it comes and goes. A visualized deity lives in the mind's eye — it can stay "out there," a picture you observe at a distance. Both can leave the practitioner as a spectator: hearing a sound, watching an image. Nyāsa shuts that gap by adding the one sense that can't keep its distance. You can hear something far away and see something far away, but you cannot *touch* something without contact. Touch is the sense of here. So when you touch the syllable into your fingertip, the mantra is no longer a thing you're aware of — it's a thing you're *in contact with*, deposited at a coordinate on your own body.[^6]

That contact does something to belief that argument can't. The body now has the mantra at specific addresses — *Śi* lives in the middle finger, the heart holds its limb-syllable, the crown is sealed. When you later chant or meditate, you're not reaching for an abstraction; you're activating something already installed. Selvalingam's framing is that the practice should make divinity *felt in the body*, not merely thought in the head — and touch is how you get it from the head into the tissue.[^7] The hand-dance and the six placements are the wiring job. Once it's wired, the god has somewhere to be when you call.

## Synergies & Handshakes

This page gives the vault the **embodiment step** of Śaiva practice — the moment where mantra leaves the air and enters flesh. The vault already holds [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nyasa-and-chakra-invocation|Nyāsa and Chakra Invocation]], which covers nyāsa in its chakra-invoking mode — placing power into the subtle centers. This page is the *companion*: nyāsa as the specific installation of *na-ma-śi-vā-ya* into the hands and six limbs. Read them together as the two halves of the practice — the chakra-invocation reaching into the subtle body, the kara/ṣaḍaṅga installation grounding the same logic in fingers and limbs you can actually feel.

It also pairs with the mantra-decoding pages. Knowing what the five syllables *mean* — their esoteric readings — is one thing; *installing* those syllables into your own hand is the move that turns the meaning into a felt charge. The decoding tells you what you're holding. The nyāsa puts it in your grip.

## Analytical Case Study: The Rap-and-Lock That Becomes Bharatanāṭyam

Selvalingam drops an aside that turns out to be load-bearing: the precise, locking hand-gestures of nyāsa are, he says, the root of Bharatanāṭyam and of Haṭha yoga — the codified dance and the codified postures both grow out of this Tantric impulse to *put the sacred into specific body-positions*.[^8] Sit with that, because it reframes two enormous traditions.

Start with the gesture itself. Kara-nyāsa is a sequence of exact hand-shapes, each holding a syllable, each landing in a fixed order — Selvalingam's "rap and lock" is precise, not loose. The hand isn't waving vaguely toward the divine; it's locking into defined positions that *mean* something, that *carry* a charge. Now look at Bharatanāṭyam's mudrās — the codified hand-shapes that compose the entire vocabulary of classical Indian dance. Each one is a fixed position with a fixed meaning. The dancer's hands speak a sacred language by locking into precise forms. That is nyāsa's logic scaled into performance: the body in exact positions, each carrying meaning and charge.

Haṭha yoga is the same impulse in the rest of the body. An āsana is a precise, held position — the whole frame locked into a shape that does something. Where nyāsa places a syllable into a fingertip, Haṭha places the practitioner into a posture, and in both cases the claim is that *the position itself is doing spiritual work*. The form is not decoration around the practice; the form *is* the practice.

What this case study reveals is the common ancestor: a conviction that divinity is installed through *precise embodiment*, not vague aspiration. You don't reach the sacred by feeling sincere. You reach it by putting your body in exact configurations that hold the charge. Nyāsa is the seed-form of that conviction — five syllables, ten fingers, six limbs, all in fixed positions. Bharatanāṭyam took the hands and ran; Haṭha took the whole body. Both are, on Selvalingam's account, nyāsa grown up. And it means that when you do kara-nyāsa, you're doing the ur-gesture of an entire embodied-sacred lineage — the small rap-and-lock from which the dance and the postures unfold.

## Implementation Workflow: The Morning Installation

It's early and quiet. You're seated, hands resting on your knees, the five syllables already turning over softly in your mouth. Then you stop chanting into the air and start placing.

You bring your right hand up. Thumb touches the tip of the index finger — *na* — and you feel the press, the small specific point of contact, and you let the syllable *land* there, as if depositing something into the fingertip. Thumb to middle finger — *ma* — another deposit. *Śi* into the next, *vā*, *ya* — five syllables, five fingertips, each one touched and charged. Your hand is no longer just a hand. It's holding the mantra at five addresses you could point to.

Now the six limbs. You touch the charged fingers to your heart — and a syllable goes home there, a warmth at the center of the chest. To the crown of the head. To the tuft at the back. You sweep the hands across the shoulders and down the arms, laying the "armor" over your torso. You touch the three eyes — both lids and the point between the brows. And then the weapon: a sharp clap, a snap, sealing the whole installation, closing the field around you like a circle drawn shut.

You sit inside it. The body is now mapped — *Śi* in the finger, a syllable at the heart, the crown sealed, the eyes charged. You're not imagining a god somewhere across the shrine. You can *feel* where the mantra lives, here, in your own tissue. When you go on to chant, the chant has somewhere to ring. The god you're worshipping is already installed in the hands you fold.

## The Nyāsa Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You'll know the installation didn't take when a few things show up.

**The touch is mechanical.** The fingers move through the sequence but nothing *lands* — no felt deposit, no charge, just a hand going through motions while the mind is elsewhere. Nyāsa without the felt contact is choreography with the soul left out. Selvalingam's whole criterion is *feeling* divinity in the body; if the touch carries no feeling, you've performed the shape and missed the placing.

**You stay a spectator.** The point of nyāsa is to close the gap between you and the deity — to stop watching a god across the room and start feeling one in your own chest. If, after the installation, the divine still feels *out there*, observed at a distance, the loop never closed. The syllables stayed in the air; they didn't enter the tissue.

**You worship the precision instead of the presence.** Because the gestures are exact, it's easy to fall in love with getting them *right* — the perfect finger sequence, the crisp seal — and lose the reason for the precision. The forms are exact because precision is how the charge gets carried, not because correctness is the goal. A flawless rap-and-lock that installs nothing is the failure dressed as success.

**You skip the body and stay in the head.** This is the deepest failure and the one nyāsa exists to prevent: doing the "practice" entirely as thought — chanting, conceptualizing, analyzing the syllables — while the body sits uninvolved. Nyāsa is the corrective to a head-only spirituality. If your hands never moved and nothing was ever touched, you didn't do nyāsa; you thought about it.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

This is one practitioner's transmission of a living ritual technique, taught in a session, not a text-critical reconstruction.[^9] The forms Selvalingam walks — kara-nyāsa, ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa, the installation of the five Śiva syllables into fingers and limbs — are standard, widely attested elements of Tantric and pūjā practice, so the *practice* itself is well-grounded even though the transmission here is single-source. The vivid claims that carry less corroboration are the *genealogical* ones: that nyāsa is specifically the root of Bharatanāṭyam and Haṭha yoga. That's a practitioner's structural-historical reading — plausible and illuminating as a claim about a shared embodied-sacred logic, but the kind of origin-claim academic history would want to qualify (codified classical dance and Haṭha have their own complex lineages). Hold the practice as solid and the grand genealogy as a suggestive, document-don't-overclaim reading.

Single-source warrant note: against the vault's scholarly Tantra sources, this is the *practitioner's* vantage — what nyāsa feels like and does from inside the ritual — which is exactly the angle text-critical scholarship tends to lack. The two warrants complement rather than compete.

Open question: if the felt charge is what makes nyāsa "work," what is the relationship between the somatic anchoring (touch installs the syllable) and the semantic content (the syllable *means* something) — does the meaning matter to the installation, or would the touch-and-sound alone do the same job?

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The plain reason these connect: nyāsa is a claim that you can change a mind by changing a body — that touching a syllable into your own hand installs a belief — and two outside fields study exactly that traffic between body and conviction.

**Psychology — embodied cognition via [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/the-self-archetype|The Self Archetype]].** The deep premise of nyāsa is that the sacred becomes *real to you* when it's located in the body, not merely entertained in the mind. That's a strong embodied-cognition claim: cognition and conviction are grounded in sensorimotor states, and a belief you can *feel in your tissue* is held differently than one you merely think. Connect this to the Self: Jung's Self is precisely what cannot be reached by intellect alone — it announces itself through symbol, image, and *felt* experience, never as a proposition you simply accept. Nyāsa is a technology for exactly that conversion — taking the divine from concept and depositing it as a felt presence at specific bodily addresses, so the Self isn't an idea you have but a charge you carry. Push the two together and something neither says by itself comes loose: where Jungian work usually waits for the felt symbol to *arise* (in dream, in active imagination), nyāsa *manufactures* the felt presence directly through touch — it's a deliberate engineering of the embodied numinous rather than a waiting for it. The mystery the depth-psychologist holds open, the tantrika installs with their own hand.

**Behavioral mechanics — anchoring and somatic conditioning.** Look at nyāsa as a behavioral procedure and it's a near-perfect anchoring protocol: you pair a deliberate physical action (touching a precise point) with a desired internal state (the felt presence of the divine), repeated daily, until the touch *itself* fires the state. That's the mechanism behind every somatic anchor — a gesture, a posture, a point of contact wired to a state through repetition, so that later the gesture alone summons the state. Nyāsa front-loads it brilliantly: it installs at *multiple* anchored points (five fingers, six limbs), so the practitioner builds not one anchor but a whole grid of them, any of which can re-fire the field. But here's the structural difference that the spiritual frame supplies and the behavioral frame can't: a behavioral anchor is *content-neutral* — you can anchor calm, confidence, focus, anything — and its value is purely functional. Nyāsa anchors a *specific cosmology*: the touch doesn't just summon a useful state, it installs the claim *this body is divine, the god lives in these hands*. So the behavioral lens explains *why nyāsa works as conditioning* — touch plus repetition plus salience builds a durable somatic trigger. The theological lens explains *why it's worth conditioning that particular thing* — because the practice is meant to recondition the subconscious toward the truth that divinity is not elsewhere. The mechanism is anchoring; the payload is non-duality.

Run the two together and you can see the whole machine. Psychology tells you *why feeling the god in the body changes belief more than thinking about the god does* — embodied cognition, the felt symbol of the Self. Behavioral mechanics tells you *how the daily touch makes the feeling reliable and re-triggerable* — anchoring across a grid of points. The combined reading: nyāsa is a precise, repeatable engineering of the embodied numinous — a technology for installing a cosmology into tissue, using the same wiring a behaviorist would recognize and aiming it at a truth a behaviorist would never name.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication.** If divinity becomes real to you by being *touched into your body*, then the head-first spirituality most modern seekers run — reading, thinking, conceptualizing, analyzing the syllables — may be precisely the thing keeping the god out of reach. Nyāsa's quiet accusation is that you cannot *think* your way into feeling divine; you have to *install* it, by hand, at specific coordinates, daily, until the body believes what the mind can only entertain. The practitioner with a flawless intellectual grasp of non-duality and an untouched body may be further from the realization than the one who simply pressed *Śi* into a fingertip every morning and felt it land.

**Generative Questions.**
1. If the felt charge is what makes nyāsa work, how much does the *meaning* of the syllable matter — would a meaningless but precisely-touched sound install the same presence, and what does your answer say about whether realization is semantic or somatic?
2. Selvalingam claims Bharatanāṭyam and Haṭha both descend from nyāsa's "put the sacred in an exact body-position" logic. Trace the same logic forward into a *secular* embodied practice (martial arts kata, a musician's hand-drills, a surgeon's muscle memory) — where does the parallel hold, and where does the "installing a cosmology" payload make nyāsa genuinely different?
3. Behavioral anchoring is content-neutral; nyāsa anchors a specific claim about reality. If you accept that any repeated gesture-plus-state will install *something*, what is your body currently being conditioned to believe by the gestures you repeat all day without intention?

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nyasa-and-chakra-invocation|Nyāsa and Chakra Invocation]] — the companion mode of nyāsa, placing power into the subtle centers; this page is the hand/six-limb installation of *na-ma-śi-vā-ya*.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/shuddhavidya-mantras-as-conscious-beings|Shuddhavidyā: Mantras as Conscious Beings]] — why installing a syllable installs a *being*, not just a sound.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/panchopachara-five-item-puja|Pañcopacāra: The Five-Item Pūjā]] — the external worship sequence that nyāsa prepares the body to perform.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/murti-focal-point-non-duality|Mūrti as Focal Point of Non-Duality]] — the deity made touchable in image; nyāsa makes the deity touchable in your own body.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-chakras-stations-of-consciousness|The Chakras: Stations of Consciousness]] — the subtle-body coordinates into which nyāsa's syllables are also installed.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/mantra-purusha-and-sphota|Mantra-Puruṣa and Sphoṭa]] — the doctrine of the body-as-mantra and sound-as-presence that nyāsa enacts.

# Siddha Alchemy — The Nāth Alchemical System

## The Body as Philosopher's Stone: Turning Flesh Into Gold From the Inside

Western alchemy became chemistry. Indian alchemy became yoga. The Western branch externalised — moving from body to crucible, from inner work to laboratory procedure, eventually forgetting the inner work altogether. The Indian branch inverted the direction and found the philosopher's stone was already inside the practitioner. The *Nāth Siddhas* of mediaeval India were the inheritors of both streams simultaneously — alchemists in the metallurgical sense, working with mercury and sulphur, and pioneers of haṭha yoga, working with breath, lock, and subtle body. They recognised these as the same work at different scales. The mercury that transmutes base metals into gold is the homologue of the semen that transmutes the mortal body into the immortal one. The outer work was a mirror. The inner work was the substance. A Siddha is a person who has completed both simultaneously — and the result is not a metaphor for gold but a literal claim: a body as hard as diamond, as luminous as the sun, as indestructible as the serpent Śeṣa who survives the dissolution of the cosmos.

## What the Nāth System Ingests

The alchemical system draws simultaneously from three traditions that the Nāths synthesised:

**Vedic sacrifice**: The fire-oblation structure (tapas as Agni, rasa as the oblation, prāṇa as Vāyu the transporter) — the internal sacrifice model providing the operational framework.

**Tantric subtle body physiology**: The bicameral body system (solar-abdominal fire/lunar-cranial nectar), Kuṇḍalinī as the working agent, the cakra hierarchy as the stages of transmutation, the nāḍī system as the plumbing.

**Metallurgical alchemy**: The specific homologies between substances — mercury as Śiva's semen / sulphur as Śakti's blood / gold as the solar metal / ash as the purified residue — providing a material vocabulary for what is being done to the body.

The synthesis is not metaphorical. The Nāths believed these three systems were running in parallel and that working with all three simultaneously accelerated the transformation beyond what any one system could achieve alone. A practitioner who did only the external alchemy had no inner transformation. A practitioner who did only the yogic work lacked the metallurgical precision. The Nāth system is deliberately overdetermined — multiple systems pointing at the same object to ensure the target is hit.

## The Seven Alchemical Stages in the Body (The Internal Logic)

Western alchemy's seven stages of transformation (calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, putrefaction, distillation, coagulation — with the final three being nigredo/blackening, albedo/whitening, rubedo/reddening representing death-purification-rebirth) have their Indian counterpart in the body's elemental hierarchy. The five gross elements (earth, water, fire, air, aether) correspond to the five lower cakras. The yogin's work is to implode each element into its superior:

**Earth → Water** (mūlādhāra → svādhiṣṭhāna): The densest, most material dimension of self begins to liquefy under the application of heat. The practitioner's grossest habits and compulsions, which have the weight and permanence of stone, begin to become fluid and workable. Kuṇḍalinī asleep at the base is the earth-solid prior to the alchemical fire.

**Water → Fire** (svādhiṣṭhāna → maṇipūra): The fluid rasa-element comes under the influence of the tapas-fire. The semen, homologised with Soma and water, begins its agitation — the prelude to being driven upward. The alchemical heat at the navel cakra is where the cooking begins.

**Fire → Air** (maṇipūra → anāhata): The fire becomes wind — the volatile, aerial quality. The prāṇic work intensifies; breath becomes the dominant operating medium. The heart cakra is where the gross body's transformation becomes perceptibly non-material.

**Air → Aether** (anāhata → viśuddha): The breath-element opens into the vast, undifferentiated space of ākāśa. This is the cakra of sound — mantra operates here; the *nāda* (vibratory resonance) of the Absolute begins to become audible internally.

**Aether → Pure Consciousness** (viśuddha → ājñā → sahasrāra): The final implosions. The subtle elements are consumed into the mind. The mind is yoked into pure Śiva-consciousness at the crown. Then this pure Śiva-consciousness is brought back to its primal unmanifest substrate — not dissolution but *return*.

What remains when the gross elements have been imploded upward through each other, leaving only aether in the cranial vault, is not nothing. It is the Siddha — the massive, powerful, perfected being who emerges from the cauldron. David Gordon White describes this: "out of the cauldron in which his lower being had been dissolved and imploded into its higher emanates — as a massive, powerful, perfected Siddha."

## The Three Perfected Bodies

The Siddha's accomplishment is not a spiritual state. It is a physiology. Three specific body-types are identified as the products of the alchemical completion:

**Divyadeha** ("divine aethereal body"): The body made of light rather than matter — the first product of the completed transmutation. It participates in the divine while remaining embodied.

**Jñānadeha** ("wisdom body"): The body constituted by and through perfect knowledge — not knowledge as information but as the direct, unmediated apprehension of the Real. The practitioner's ontological status is determined by their epistemic state.

**Siddhadeha** ("magical body"): The body of accomplished powers — the *vajradeha* (diamond-thunderbolt body) that has the *vajrakāyasiddhi* (power of body as hard as diamond). This body is what the *Rasāṇava* text describes in its extraordinary portrait of the perfect Siddha: "His body is a bolt of lightning amidst the storm clouds of his curling jet-black hair. As immaculate as the chaplain of the gods, he is an alchemical wizard and wonder-worker."

These are not three separate goals. They are three descriptions of the same accomplished state from three different angles: energetic (divyadeha), epistemic (jñānadeha), and material (siddhadeha).

## The Jivanmukta: Liberated While Living

*Jivanmukta* (living liberated being) is the tradition's term for someone who has completed the alchemical work while still in the body. This is importantly different from liberation through death (which is the deal most traditions offer — you transcend when you leave the body behind). The Nāth Siddha tradition claims transcendence is fully achievable *in* the body, *through* the body, *as* the body — not by abandoning it but by transmuting it. The body is not the obstacle to liberation. The uninflamed, uncompleted body is the obstacle. The fully alchemised body is the vehicle of liberation itself.

This jivanmukta exists in a specific relationship to the cosmos: he is liberated from karma and rebirth but *not dissolved into the Absolute* (which would be mokṣa — the goal of some Advaita systems). He retains individuality. He is like a Siddha mountain peak — identifiable, individual, exempted from the lower worlds of rebirth but not absorbed into formlessness. He is *free within the cosmos* rather than free *from* the cosmos.

## The Mughal Institutional Afterlife: When the Alchemical Mercury Became a Trade Good

White's *Sinister Yogis* (2009) adds the dimension the inner-alchemy account leaves out: the *institutional-economic* life of the Nāth Siddhas in the Mughal period, where the alchemical mercury became a literal trade commodity. The Nāth Yogīs were, across the 14th–19th centuries, not only inner-alchemists but a powerful warrior-merchant-banking order — "at first traders in horses and elephants," expanding through "land grants, control of temples and pilgrimage sites, warfare, and, eventually, banking," placing chosen princes on the thrones of Marwar and Nepal.[^3] And the *same mercury* that was the alchemical substance (Śiva's semen, the agent of inner transmutation) was a Nāth *trade good*: the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb signed an imperial edict offering "his continued protection to a Nāth Yog monastery and its land grants in the Punjab in exchange for treated quicksilver."[^4] The inner work and the outer economy meet in the mercury — the substance the Siddha circulates in his subtle body is the substance the Nāth order *sold to emperors*. This institutional afterlife reframes the alchemy: the Nāth Siddha was not only a solitary inner-transmuter but a member of an order whose alchemical expertise was also a *commercial asset* (longevity drugs, aphrodisiacs, treated mercury sold to kings) and whose pursuit of the *diamond body* (vajradeha) ran alongside a pursuit of worldly power (kingmaking, banking, land). The same orders that taught the inner philosopher's-stone work were the warrior-banker institutions that dominated north Indian credit by the 1780s — the inner alchemy and the outer empire were two faces of one Nāth institution. (See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nath-yogis-as-warrior-merchants-bankers-mughal-period-institutional-architecture|Nāth Yogis as Warrior-Merchants-Bankers]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/yogi-as-alchemist-healer-poisoner-aphrodisiac-merchant-prince-corpus|Yogi as Alchemist-Healer-Poisoner]].)

## Tensions

The most contested element of Nāth alchemy is the *semen transmutation* claim — that semen physically rises through the sushumna nāḍī and condenses in the cranial vault as amṛta. Modern physiology does not support the literal claim in anatomical terms. The tradition's response is that the subtle body is a different register of reality than the gross body, and that the "semen" that moves is the subtle essence (*sukra-tattva*) corresponding to but not identical with the physical fluid. This is either a principled metaphysical claim or a post-hoc rationalisation — the distinction matters a great deal for practice.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

The Nāth alchemical claim has one implication that cuts across every other spirituality or self-improvement framework: **the goal is not to become a better version of your current self. It is to incinerate the current self and build something else from the ash.** Most development frameworks are additive — you learn new skills, adopt better habits, cultivate improved patterns. The alchemical model is subtractive-then-constructive: you burn down to ash, and something new grows from the ash. The thing that grows is not continuous with what was burned. The Siddha does not remember being the Paśu the way the 30-year-old remembers being a teenager. The transformation is categorical, not incremental. This means that incremental self-improvement is not the path — it is the *avoidance* of the path, the substitution of gradual refinement for the terrifying commitment to genuine transmutation. The question the alchemical model asks is not "are you improving?" but "have you lit the fire?"

**Generative Questions**

- The alchemical work implodes each element into its superior — earth becomes water, water becomes fire — until only aether remains. If you map this onto the layers of your creative identity (the most material/mechanical competencies at the bottom, the most evanescent/ineffable capacities at the top): what is the earth in your practice, and what would happen if it was forced to become water? What densities are you protecting from the fire's liquefying effect?
- The Nāths were simultaneously metallurgical alchemists and yogic practitioners — external and internal work running in parallel, each as a mirror of the other. What is the external practice in your life that mirrors the internal transformation you are supposedly working toward? If there is no external mirror, is the internal work actually happening?
- The jivanmukta is liberated but retains individuality — not dissolved into formlessness but exempted from the lower world's gravitational pull. What would it mean to operate from a position of genuine exemption from the conditioning forces that currently shape your creative choices — not transcendence of the world but freedom *within* it?

## War Yoga (Billinge) Enrichment — The Three Bodies, the Path of Essence, and the Wizard's Apparatus
*Added 2026-06-03, Billinge re-ingest.*

Billinge names the **goal-bodies** the Nāth adept is building toward: a **divyadeha** ("divine aethereal body"), a **jñānadeha** ("wisdom body"), a **siddhadeha** ("magical body") — together "a receptacle worthy of a jivanmukta."[^5] The road to them is the **rasāyana**, the "path of essence," which "aims to extract the divine essence from the gross corporeal body" — a discipline "of internal alchemy, of transmutation and bodily transubstantiation."[^5] Siddhis and jivanmukti are "the direct result of internal combustion and transformation of sexual fluids into amṛta."[^5]

The mechanism gets a literal piece of lab equipment behind it: the yogic body is the **vidyādhara yantra** ("wizard's apparatus"), and Billinge maps it onto an actual alchemical still — "the upward sublimation apparatus of alchemy is made of two vessels. A slow fire fed with cow dung below the lower vessel heats herbs and mercury ore. Mercury then evaporates upwards, condensing in the upper chamber." Just so, "the abdominal fire chamber heats semen, which is cooled and condensed in the cooling chamber: the cranial vault."[^5] The outer still and the inner body are the *same machine*.

And the metals carry the gods: "Mercury is the semen of the phallic god Śiva: the sexual essence of the absolute. Sulphur is the uterine blood of the goddess Śakti. Gold is the perfect solar metal" — and "in order to be absorbed, gold must be purified and fixed with mercury (rasa), the quintessence of Śiva."[^5] White's line, which Billinge leans on, fixes the goal: the outer work of "transmuting vulgar metals to gold is the mirror of the inner work of extracting from his material manifestation the autonomous Spirit, which shares the same essence as gold."[^5] This deepens the page's mercury=semen homology by supplying the *apparatus* (the wizard's still), the *path* (rasāyana), and the *three goal-bodies* the vajradeha completes. `[PARAPHRASED — Billinge synthesis]` applies to the WarYoga framing (the Sanctus Europa trust-flag); the divyadeha/jñānadeha/siddhadeha, rasāyana, vidyādhara-yantra, and the metal-god mappings are White-sourced (*The Alchemical Body*).

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/rasa-management-fluid-alchemy|Rasa Management — The Fluid Alchemy]] — the rasa system is the raw material of Nāth alchemy; semen-as-Soma is the central working substance
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/tapas-as-spiritual-catalyst|Tapas as Spiritual Catalyst]] — the fire of the alchemical work; calcination requires heat
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/pashu-vira-siddha-spectrum|Paśu-Virā-Siddha Spectrum]] — the Siddha is the completed alchemical product; the spectrum is the developmental map, alchemy is the mechanism
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/pranahagnihotra-breath-sacrifice|Prāṇāgnihotra — Breath as Continuous Sacrifice]] — prāṇa is the wind that carries the alchemical fire; without breath control, the transmutation cannot proceed
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/skambha-and-the-cosmo-body|Skambha and the Cosmo-Body]] — the bicameral body architecture (solar abdomen/lunar cranium) is the alchemical vessel; the spine-pillar is the axis of the work
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/siddhis-and-the-attainment-trap|Siddhis and the Attainment Trap]] — siddhis are byproducts of the alchemical process; the attainment trap is stopping the work to enjoy the powers it generates

## Footnotes

[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/siddhis-and-the-attainment-trap|Siddhis and the Attainment Trap]] — the broader context for the Nāth alchemical system and its relationship to siddhis as byproducts.
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/white-sinister-yogis|David Gordon White — Sinister Yogis]] (2009), lines 10024-10045 — the Nāth Yogīs as warrior-merchant-banker order (horses/elephants → land grants → banking; kingmaking in Marwar and Nepal).
[^4]: White, *Sinister Yogis* (2009), lines 9671-9678 — Aurangzeb's edict protecting a Nāth monastery in exchange for treated quicksilver.
